paragraphs: Sparse learning uses penalties that encourage a model to retain only a limited set of useful components. Non-convex penalties have theoretical advantages over convex alternatives in several settings, but optimizing them is difficult. A common approach replaces the original problem with a sequence of convex problems, making the overall computation expensive for large datasets.

The paper introduces General Iterative Shrinkage and Thresholding, or GIST, for a broad class of these penalties. Each iteration solves a proximal operator problem, which combines an update with the effect of the penalty. For many commonly used penalties, that smaller problem has a closed-form solution. A line search, initialized using the Barzilai-Borwein rule, helps find an appropriate step size quickly.

The contribution combines this computational strategy with a detailed convergence analysis. Experiments on large datasets demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency. The practical significance is that useful non-convex penalties can be approached through relatively direct iterative updates, reducing the computational burden associated with repeatedly solving convex surrogate problems.
icml-2013-a-general-iterative-shrinkage-.tldr: GIST makes optimization with many non-convex sparsity penalties more practical through simple proximal updates and an efficient step-size search.

paragraphs: The paper studies semi-supervised learning when both inputs and outputs have structure. The goal is to learn a relationship between them using a formulation that can accommodate more than a single scalar prediction. It expresses this problem through a vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert space, providing a common mathematical setting for the learning task.

Within that setting, vector-valued manifold regularization and multi-view learning appear as special cases. This connection matters because it brings approaches concerned with data structure and multiple input views into one formulation. The contribution is therefore broader than an individual prediction method: it identifies a shared framework in which these approaches can be expressed and connected.

For least-squares loss, the authors derive a closed-form solution and provide an efficient implementation. Experiments on challenging multiclass categorization problems find that the multi-view formulation performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods and significantly better than single-view learning. Those findings support the value of combining views within the proposed framework on the evaluated tasks.
icml-2013-a-unifying-framework-for-vecto.tldr: A vector-valued kernel framework unifies manifold regularization and multi-view learning, with an efficient closed-form solution for least-squares loss.

paragraphs: Documents often belong to categories nested inside larger categories. This paper develops topic-model inference for corpora with such multilevel organization. It takes a parametric approach, assuming that the number of topics is known or can be selected through cross-validation. The models are finite-dimensional special cases of hierarchical Dirichlet processes.

The central technical contribution is a simple variational approximation that handles dependence between latent Dirichlet variables at neighboring levels of the hierarchy. A previously unused inequality makes that approximation possible. This matters because inference must account for how adjacent levels relate, rather than treating the document hierarchy as merely an external organizational label.

On several benchmarks, the approach runs faster than Gibbs sampling and learns more predictive models than existing variational methods. The authors also demonstrate large-scale use on two computer-security corpora: one containing 350,000 documents and more than 6,000 internal subcategories, and another with five hierarchical levels. These results support both the inference method's practical efficiency and its applicability to substantial hierarchical collections.
icml-2013-a-variational-approximation-fo.tldr: A new variational approximation enables efficient topic modeling of hierarchical document collections when the number of topics is fixed or selected in advance.

paragraphs: A sampling process can struggle to move between distinct modes, or separate regions where data are concentrated. This paper investigates whether a learned representation can make those movements easier. Its starting point is the hypothesis, supported by earlier experimental evidence, that well-trained deeper representations tend to separate underlying factors of variation more effectively.

The authors explore the related conjecture that this disentangling can produce Markov chains that mix faster between modes. They also propose a geometric explanation: at higher representation levels, samples may occupy their space more uniformly, while high-density manifolds become less folded. Under this picture, movement through the representation could connect regions that are harder to traverse in the original space.

The paper examines these ideas through visualizations, measurements of movement between modes, and interpolation between samples. Its contribution is an experimental investigation of a possible link between representation quality and sampling behavior. The claims remain hypotheses under study, rather than a guarantee that increasing network depth will always improve mixing.
icml-2013-better-mixing-via-deep-represe.tldr: The paper experimentally investigates whether disentangled deep representations help sampling chains move more efficiently between modes.

paragraphs: Kernel methods rely on the representer theorem to preserve optimality when solving penalized empirical risk minimization problems. In this setting, the training objective combines fit to observed data with a regularizer. Whether the theorem applies depends on the form of that regularizer, making its conditions central to the mathematical justification of the method.

Previously known conditions were sufficient: meeting them guaranteed the theorem, but did not completely identify when it could hold. This paper supplies a full characterization through necessary and sufficient conditions on the regularizer. That distinction matters because a complete characterization describes the boundary of applicability, rather than only a collection of safe choices.

The authors report that the resulting conditions are simple and broaden the settings where the representer theorem is known to apply. They also address an extension to matrices. The contribution is therefore a sharper foundation for choosing regularizers in kernel-based optimization, together with consideration of how that foundation extends beyond the original domain.
icml-2013-characterizing-the-representer.tldr: The paper completely characterizes the regularizer conditions that ensure the representer theorem holds and addresses an extension to matrices.

paragraphs: Clustering and community detection often involve choosing a set that minimizes a ratio of two set-based quantities while satisfying constraints. These problems are typically NP-hard. Convex or spectral relaxations make them easier to optimize, but their solutions can be far from the original optimum when the relaxed problem is too loosely connected to the discrete one.

The paper proves that every constrained ratio-minimization problem involving non-negative set functions admits a tight relaxation into an unconstrained continuous problem. This establishes a general route from constrained set selection to continuous optimization. The non-negativity condition is part of the stated result, and the tightness addresses the quality of the reformulation itself.

The resulting continuous problem is non-convex, so the method does not guarantee finding its global optimum. Nevertheless, experiments on constrained local clustering show a large advantage over the looser convex and spectral alternatives. The contribution combines a broad reformulation theorem with evidence that accepting harder continuous optimization can yield substantially better clustering solutions.
icml-2013-constrained-fractional-set-pro.tldr: Constrained ratios of non-negative set functions admit tight continuous relaxations that improve local clustering results, although global optimization remains unguaranteed.

paragraphs: Collective classification makes predictions in a setting where relationships among examples matter. This paper considers how to perform that task when a malicious adversary can alter input attributes. The threat model is specific: the attributes are binary, and the adversary may modify no more than a fixed number of them.

The authors formulate robust learning as a convex quadratic program. Within this formulation, they guarantee optimal weights against a worst-case adversary, with polynomial-time computation. The fixed modification budget gives the optimization a defined set of attacks to protect against, making the robustness objective precise rather than leaving adversarial behavior unrestricted.

The paper also observes that adversarial regularization can improve generalization even when no attacker is present. Experiments on real and simulated data consistently outperform both non-adversarial and non-relational baselines. Together, these findings support combining relational prediction with explicit worst-case protection, while the formal guarantee remains tied to the stated binary-attribute attack model.
icml-2013-convex-adversarial-collective-.tldr: A convex quadratic program learns collective-classification weights that are optimal against a worst-case adversary with a fixed binary-attribute modification budget.

paragraphs: Online optimization evaluates a learner by comparing its accumulated loss with that of a reference sequence of decisions. Existing tracking-regret bounds often grow with how much that sequence changes. In a nonstationary environment, however, a useful reference may need to change substantially, making low-variation comparisons a poor reflection of the task.

The paper introduces dynamic mirror descent with a family of candidate dynamical models. The method tracks a suitable model and uses it to form predictions. Its regret bounds depend on how far the comparator departs from the best dynamics in the family, shifting attention from the total amount of change to how well that change follows a model.

This distinction allows low regret relative to highly variable comparator sequences when their evolution is sufficiently well captured by the candidate dynamics. The authors demonstrate the idea using sequential compressive observations of a changing scene and tracking a dynamic social network. The contribution is a way to exploit predictable structure within nonstationarity.
icml-2013-dynamical-models-and-tracking-.tldr: Dynamic mirror descent bounds tracking regret through mismatch with candidate dynamical models, allowing meaningful comparisons with rapidly changing reference sequences.

paragraphs: A disjunction is a rule that accepts an example when at least one of its constituent conditions holds. This paper studies how to learn such rules efficiently in a semi-supervised setting, where the learning problem includes unlabeled information. The algorithms operate under a stated regularity assumption, so the results concern a structured learning setting.

The authors prove sample-complexity bounds under an additional mild restriction on the data distribution. These bounds describe how much data the algorithms require to learn. They also develop an active learning algorithm with improved sample complexity, connecting the learning task to a setting in which the learner can select examples for labeling.

All of the algorithms are extended to random classification noise, addressing labels that may be randomly corrupted. The contribution therefore covers efficient learning, data requirements, and a noisy-label extension within one family of prediction rules. Its guarantees depend on the stated regularity and distributional conditions; the abstract does not claim unrestricted learnability for arbitrary data.
icml-2013-efficient-semi-supervised-and-.tldr: The paper gives efficient semi-supervised and active algorithms for learning disjunctions under stated assumptions, including extensions to random label noise.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning assigns labels to bags of observations without fully identifying the labels inside each bag. Negative bags contain only negative instances, while positive bags leave uncertainty about which instances are positive. The proposed eMIL method builds this asymmetry into a large-margin classifier that represents bags using ellipsoids.

The authors derive a distance between an ellipsoid and a separating hyperplane, generalizing the support vector machine setting. Negative bags are handled as uncertain observations through robust optimization, while positive bags may cross the margin. They also establish that ellipsoidal representations under this distance are the most robust solution when a bag is treated as a random variable with finite mean and covariance.

Two algorithms address the resulting non-convex problem: a concave-convex procedure and a quasi-Newton method. The approach achieves competitive benchmark results and outperforms competing methods on a newly introduced wheel-defect dataset based on multiple partial observations. These findings support modeling bag-level uncertainty while respecting the different meanings of positive and negative labels.
icml-2013-ellipsoidal-multiple-instance-.tldr: eMIL represents bags as ellipsoids and treats positive and negative bags differently to build a robust large-margin multiple instance classifier.

paragraphs: A multivariate time series contains several signals evolving together over time. Forecastable Component Analysis, or ForeCA, reduces their dimension by focusing on forecastability. The paper introduces a measure of that property and uses it to determine a transformation of the original signals, making temporal predictability the organizing objective of the representation.

The transformation separates the series into a forecastable space and an orthogonal white-noise space. This gives the method a specific purpose: distinguish components with forecastable structure from a separate noise component. The author presents a converging algorithm with a fast eigenvector solution, connecting the proposed measure to a practical way of finding the transformation.

Applications to financial and macroeconomic series show that ForeCA can identify informative structure useful for forecasting and classification. Those applications demonstrate the potential value of the extracted components for more than one prediction task. An accompanying R package is also reported. The stated findings support forecastability as a useful criterion for reducing the dimension of temporally dependent data.
icml-2013-forecastable-component-analysi.tldr: ForeCA reduces multivariate time series into forecastable components and an orthogonal white-noise space using a new forecastability measure.

paragraphs: Copulas separate the modeling of individual variables from the modeling of their dependence. Vine constructions make high-dimensional dependence more manageable by assembling a hierarchy of conditional two-variable copulas. A common simplification assumes that each such copula does not change with the values of the variables on which it is conditioned.

This paper relaxes that simplification. It learns latent functions that determine a conditional copula's shape from its conditioning variables, allowing the dependence pattern itself to vary with context. The authors use a Bayesian approach based on sparse Gaussian processes, together with expectation propagation for scalable approximate inference.

Experiments on real datasets show better estimates of the underlying copula when all conditional dependencies are modeled. The result supports retaining information that the usual simplifying assumption discards. The contribution is both representational and computational: it allows richer conditional dependence while supplying an approximate inference method intended to make that richer model practical.
icml-2013-gaussian-process-vine-copulas-.tldr: Sparse Gaussian processes let vine copulas adapt their dependence patterns to conditioning variables, improving copula estimates in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies online learning with partial feedback, where a decision's utility is not observed directly. Instead, the learner must estimate properties of the environment and use those estimates to assess decisions. This makes information gathering central: observations are useful because of what they reveal about the parameters underlying the utility.

The authors propose a generic pure-exploration algorithm that accommodates different utility functions. Its scope includes settings ranging from ordinary multi-armed bandits to dueling bandits. The common framework connects these problems through the estimation process needed to evaluate choices, rather than requiring a separate formulation for every way of defining utility.

The main application generalizes dueling bandits to a mixed crowd whose members have individual preferences. Environment parameters represent that preference diversity, allowing the learning problem to reflect more than one uniform viewpoint. The contribution is a shared exploration approach and a voting-bandit setting for such populations, extending the range of preference-based decisions that can be expressed within the framework.
icml-2013-generic-exploration-and-k-arme.tldr: A generic pure-exploration framework handles utilities inferred from environment parameters, including voting-bandit problems involving diverse crowd preferences.

paragraphs: Bandit problems become challenging when the learner faces large state and action spaces. This paper studies parametric versions of those problems and asks what supervised learning capability can support their solution. The central result is an algorithmic reduction to the supervised learning framework called Knows What It Knows, or KWIK.

A reduction establishes a way to solve one learning problem using a method for another. Here, it connects large-scale bandit learning to KWIK learnability, providing a common requirement around which algorithms can be built. The authors also prove matching impossibility results: weaker supervised learning assumptions cannot replace the KWIK requirement in the settings they examine.

Both sides of the result apply to the standard parametric bandit setting and to a new setting where the action set is finite but grows over time. The contribution therefore identifies both an algorithmic route and a boundary on weakening its learning assumptions. The growing-action model extends this connection to problems whose available choices expand during interaction.
icml-2013-large-scale-bandit-problems-an.tldr: Large parametric bandit problems reduce to KWIK learning, with matching impossibility results showing why weaker supervised learning assumptions do not suffice.

paragraphs: A person or animal controlling a system may act using an internal understanding that differs from the system's true dynamics. This paper seeks to recover that internal model from control demonstrations and known task goals. The distinction matters because behavior can reflect what the subject believes the system will do, rather than its actual behavior.

Sensory feedback delay is central to the framework. Because current feedback is unavailable immediately, the subject uses an internal model to predict the present state, and that prediction may differ from reality. The authors develop a probabilistic framework and an exact expectation-maximization algorithm that jointly estimate the internal dynamics, internal state trajectories, and feedback delay.

They apply the method to brain-machine interface control demonstrated by a nonhuman primate. The inferred internal model differs from the actual interface dynamics and explains recorded neural control signals significantly better than the true dynamics do. This finding supports explicitly modeling the subject's internal prediction process when interpreting the observed control signals.
icml-2013-learning-an-internal-dynamics-.tldr: A probabilistic method infers a subject's internal dynamics and feedback delay, better explaining neural control signals in the reported brain-machine interface application.

paragraphs: Matrix approximation uses observed entries to build a compact account of a larger matrix. It appears in recommendation, text mining, and computer vision. A common modeling assumption is that the partially observed matrix has low rank, meaning that its overall structure can be represented through a limited number of underlying components.

This paper replaces the global assumption with a local one: the matrix is assumed to have low-rank structure locally. The resulting model represents the observed matrix as a weighted sum of low-rank matrices. This allows several component approximations to contribute to the overall representation, rather than requiring one low-rank approximation to describe the entire matrix.

The authors analyze the accuracy of this local modeling approach and evaluate it on recommendation tasks. Their experiments show improved prediction accuracy over classical approaches. The findings support the usefulness of the local low-rank assumption in those tasks, where combining simpler component models provides a more effective approximation of the observed data.
icml-2013-local-low-rank-matrix-approxim.tldr: Modeling a matrix as a weighted combination of locally low-rank components improves recommendation prediction accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Studying viral text involves two connected questions: how information spreads through a network, and how to track the memes being spread. This paper addresses diffusion-network inference and meme tracking together. Combining them in one model provides a shared probabilistic account of the spread process and the content being followed.

The model uses a mixture of mutually exciting point processes. This represents diffusion through events whose occurrence can encourage other events, with the mixture supplying multiple components in the model. The authors develop a fast learning algorithm based on mean-field variational inference and a budgeted diffusion bandwidth, connecting the probabilistic formulation to a computational procedure.

The approach is demonstrated on viral text in online social networks, including Twitter, and in the web's blogosphere. These applications illustrate the joint treatment of network inference and meme tracking across two diffusion settings. The stated contribution is the ability to address both tasks simultaneously, together with an inference approach and application demonstrations.
icml-2013-mixture-of-mutually-exciting-p.tldr: A mixture of mutually exciting point processes jointly models diffusion networks and meme tracking, with demonstrations on social-network and blog text.

paragraphs: Standard latent Dirichlet allocation assumes that its vocabulary is defined before learning begins. That is workable for a fixed document collection, but awkward for streams in which previously unseen terms continue to arrive. This paper extends the topic model so that new words can become part of its representation during online learning.

Instead of drawing topics from a finite Dirichlet distribution, the model draws them from a Dirichlet process with a base distribution over all strings. Computation still requires a finite set of represented words for each truncated topic. The authors therefore combine online variational inference with heuristics that organize, expand, and shrink those finite vocabulary representations.

The results show that the model successfully incorporates newly encountered terms. It also performs better than online LDA in the reported evaluations of topic quality and classification. The approach's significance is the combination of an open-ended vocabulary model with a changing finite computational representation, making vocabulary growth part of online topic learning.
icml-2013-online-latent-dirichlet-alloca.tldr: An online LDA extension admits previously unseen words through an open-ended vocabulary model and dynamically managed finite topic representations.

paragraphs: The paper considers an agent learning from one uninterrupted sequence of actions, observations, and rewards, without resets. The environment itself need not be a Markov decision process. Instead, the agent has several ways to map its interaction history into discrete states, only some of which produce a valid Markov representation.

The learner must choose among these representations while also learning unknown dynamics. Its regret is measured against an agent that already knows a Markov representation with the highest optimal reward and acts optimally within it. This comparison combines the cost of discovering a useful state description with the cost of learning how to act.

The proposed algorithm achieves regret of order square root of T after T steps, improving on the earlier T-to-the-two-thirds rate described in the abstract. It also avoids the earlier bound's additive term exponential in characteristics of the optimal model, with constants described as reasonably small. The dependence on T is optimal because the same square-root rate is optimal even for learning within a single discrete Markov decision process.
icml-2013-optimal-regret-bounds-for-sele.tldr: An algorithm selects among candidate state representations while learning to act, achieving regret with optimal square-root dependence on interaction length.

paragraphs: Metric learning transforms data so that distances better serve a prediction task, such as ranking or nearest-neighbor classification. The paper focuses on a difficulty that arises when many input features carry little useful information. In that setting, existing methods can fail to identify the relevant features, and prediction quality deteriorates.

The proposed method learns a linear transformation while imposing group sparsity on it. This structural constraint encourages selective use of groups within the transformation. At the same time, training optimizes structured ranking output prediction, tying the learned representation to the ranking task it is intended to support.

The authors present the algorithm as efficient and robust, and evaluate it on synthetic and real datasets. It outperforms previous methods in both high-noise and low-noise settings in those experiments. The contribution is the combination of structural feature selection and task-oriented metric learning, with evidence that the combination helps across the evaluated noise conditions.
icml-2013-robust-structural-metric-learn.tldr: Group sparsity helps a ranking-oriented metric learner handle uninformative features, outperforming previous methods in the reported noise settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear classification when the learned function must be discrete. Given positively and negatively labeled feature vectors, the training objective is to minimize their cumulative hinge loss. The discrete restriction makes this a combinatorial optimization problem, and the paper identifies the resulting task as NP-hard.

The authors propose two simple rounding algorithms that convert a fractional solution into a discrete one. This separates the search for a fractional solution from the step that enforces discreteness. Approximation bounds for the rounding methods help characterize the consequences of that conversion, connecting a practical procedure to a theoretical account of its quality.

The paper also derives generalization bounds for two important classes of linear functions with binary weights. It does so by establishing their Rademacher complexity and combining that analysis with rounding guarantees. Comparisons on synthetic and real-world data complement the theory. The contribution thus addresses both how to construct discrete classifiers and how to analyze their behavior beyond training examples.
icml-2013-rounding-methods-for-discrete-.tldr: Two rounding algorithms turn fractional solutions into discrete linear classifiers, supported by approximation and generalization bounds.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to maximize a function globally when only a finite number of noisy evaluations are available. Its assumption is local: near at least one global maximum, the function must be smooth in a specified sense relative to some semi-metric. The algorithm does not need to know that semi-metric.

Stochastic Simultaneous Optimistic Optimization, or StoSOO, organizes the search through hierarchical partitions of the domain. It repeatedly constructs upper confidence bounds and uses them to decide which point to evaluate next. The optimistic strategy directs evaluations using what regions could plausibly offer, while accounting for uncertainty introduced by noisy observations.

A finite-time analysis shows performance almost as good as the best specifically tuned algorithms, despite the unknown local smoothness. This makes adaptation the central contribution: the learner can search effectively without receiving the smoothness information that specialized methods use. The guarantee remains conditional on the stated local regularity around a global maximum.
icml-2013-stochastic-simultaneous-optimi.tldr: StoSOO uses optimistic hierarchical search to approach tuned algorithms' performance under noisy evaluations without knowing the function's local smoothness.

paragraphs: Many datasets combine observations with different meanings: numbers, categories, ordered responses, and rankings. Thurstonian Boltzmann Machines provide a unified architecture for handling such inputs together. The motivating idea is that many discrete observations can be understood as outcomes generated from underlying continuous variables that are not directly observed.

Each discrete observation constrains those hidden variables through inequalities. Learning and inference then work with the resulting collection of constraints. This supplies a shared representation for otherwise different data types, including Gaussian observations, intervals, censored values, binary and categorical responses, multiple categories, ordinal data, and complete or incomplete rankings with or without ties.

The authors demonstrate the model on handwritten digit recognition, collaborative filtering, and complex social survey analysis. These applications illustrate the architecture's versatility across substantially different tasks. The contribution lies in using latent continuous variables and inequality constraints as a common modeling language, allowing heterogeneous observations to participate within the same learning framework.
icml-2013-thurstonian-boltzmann-machines.tldr: Thurstonian Boltzmann Machines unify varied observation types by expressing discrete data as inequality constraints on latent continuous variables.

paragraphs: Stratified Monte Carlo integration divides a domain into regions and samples within each region to estimate an integral. This paper considers a finite budget of noisy function evaluations. It addresses two decisions together: how to partition the domain and how many samples to assign to each resulting region.

Those decisions create a tradeoff. Finer partitions can reduce variability where the function or observation noise is heterogeneous. But dividing too finely makes it harder to allocate the available samples close to an oracle strategy. A useful partition must therefore balance the benefit of finer distinctions against the difficulty of distributing limited observations effectively.

The proposed Monte-Carlo Upper-Lower Confidence Bound algorithm chooses a partition online from a large class of candidates. It selects one with a near-optimal tradeoff and allocates samples almost optimally within it. The contribution is joint adaptation of the sampling regions and their budgets, recognizing that neither choice can be judged independently of the other.
icml-2013-toward-optimal-stratification-.tldr: An adaptive Monte Carlo algorithm jointly selects a near-optimal partition and an almost-optimal sample allocation under a finite noisy-evaluation budget.

paragraphs: A set of data points can be described through polynomial relationships that equal zero at every point. The collection of all such polynomials is called its vanishing ideal. Although that collection can be large, a small set of generator polynomials can represent it compactly, offering a way to describe nonlinear structure in the data.

The paper develops and analyzes an efficient procedure for constructing these generators. The procedure is numerically stable and also supports polynomials that vanish approximately, rather than requiring their values to be exactly zero. This extends the representation from exact algebraic relationships to relationships that hold approximately across the observed points.

The resulting polynomials can be used in supervised learning. In empirical comparisons with kernel methods, the approach produces more compact classifiers with comparable accuracy. The finding supports polynomial generators as a useful representation for classification: they capture nonlinear relationships while allowing a smaller classifier in the reported comparisons, without a corresponding loss of comparable predictive accuracy.
icml-2013-vanishing-component-analysis-e.tldr: Vanishing Component Analysis learns compact polynomial descriptions of nonlinear data structure, yielding smaller classifiers with accuracy comparable to kernel methods in experiments.
